# Glossary {#glossary}

Plain-language definitions of the terms used across this wiki. Terms tagged
[SORTEE]{.tada-gloss-tag} follow the glossary in the SORTEE guidelines (Table 1;
[Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}). The rest are our own
definitions. Where a chapter covers a term in depth, the definition links to it.

::: {.tada-glossary}

[Absolute path]{#gloss-absolute-path data-match="absolute path|absolute file path|local file path|hard-coded path"}
:   A file path written out in full from the top of one computer's file system,
    such as `C:/Users/ed/Desktop/data.csv`. Also called a local or hard-coded
    path. It only exists on that machine, so code that uses one fails for
    everyone else. Compare *relative path*. See
    [Transferable](#transferable-paths).

[Analytical code]{#gloss-analytical-code data-match="analytical code"}
:   Code written to analyse one dataset for one study. Its job is to be a
    transparent, reproducible record of that analysis, not a tool for other
    people. Compare *software*. See [TADA at a glance](#tada-why).

[Annotated]{#gloss-annotated}
:   The fourth TADA principle: comments inside the code say what each chunk
    does, why, and where its output appears in the paper. See
    [Annotated](#annotated).

[Archiving]{#gloss-archiving} [SORTEE]{.tada-gloss-tag}
:   Depositing data and code in a public repository. Archiving is not the same
    as putting files on GitHub or in supplementary material; see *immutable*
    and *persistent identifier*.

[Available]{#gloss-available}
:   The second TADA principle: the code is publicly archived with a persistent
    identifier that is cited in the paper. See [Available](#available).

[CC0 and CC BY]{#gloss-cc data-match="CC0|CC BY|CC-BY"}
:   Two Creative Commons licences, common for data. CC0 places work in the
    public domain with no conditions. CC BY lets others reuse the work as long
    as they credit you. Neither is designed for code. See
    [Licences](#sharing-licences).

[Code review]{#gloss-code-review data-match="code review"}
:   Checking and evaluating each other's code, either formally during peer
    review or informally among co-authors and colleagues. See
    [Code review](#code-review).

[Computational reproducibility]{#gloss-computational-reproducibility data-match="computational reproducibility|computationally reproducible|computationally reproduced"}
:   Obtaining consistent results using the same input data, computational
    methods and conditions of analysis, the definition the SORTEE guidelines
    use. In practice, it means getting the paper's results by running its
    archived code on its archived data. This is Stage 6 of the
    [SORTEE guidelines](#sortee-stages).

[Container]{#gloss-container data-match="container|containerisation|Docker|Apptainer|Singularity"}
:   An image that packages a complete software environment, including all the
    programs and libraries your code needs, so it runs the same way on another
    computer. Docker and Apptainer are the common tools.
    Beyond the scope of TADA.

[Copyleft licence]{#gloss-copyleft data-match="copyleft|GPL"}
:   A licence that requires anything built from your code to be released under
    the same licence. The GPL is the usual example. Compare *permissive
    licence*.

[Data and code quality control]{#gloss-quality-control data-match="quality control|quality-control"} [SORTEE]{.tada-gloss-tag}
:   Checking whether data and code are suitable for public archiving. It is not
    a code review: it does not judge whether the analysis is correct. See
    [The SORTEE guidelines](#sortee).

[Data availability statement]{#gloss-das data-match="data availability statement|data and code availability"}
:   The section of a paper that says where the data and code are archived and
    how to access them, usually with their DOIs.

[Data dictionary]{#gloss-data-dictionary data-match="data dictionary|data dictionaries|codebook"}
:   A file listing every variable in a dataset with its description and units.
    Also called a codebook. A form of *metadata*.

[Data editor]{#gloss-data-editor data-match="data editor"} [SORTEE]{.tada-gloss-tag}
:   An editor at a journal whose job is to screen and quality-control the data
    and code that will be archived alongside papers under review.

[Data filtering]{#gloss-filtering data-match="data filtering|filtered data"} [SORTEE]{.tada-gloss-tag}
:   Removing some data to create the dataset used in the analysis, for example
    removing individuals with a certain characteristic. The result is
    *filtered data*.

[Data processing]{#gloss-processing data-match="data processing|processed data"} [SORTEE]{.tada-gloss-tag}
:   Transforming data from one form to another: extracting data from images or
    videos, summarising, transforming or calculating new values. The result is
    *processed data*. Typing up a field sheet does not count.

[Dependency]{#gloss-dependency data-match="dependency|dependencies"}
:   A package or library that your code needs in order to run.

[DOI]{#gloss-doi data-match="DOI"}
:   Digital Object Identifier. A persistent identifier for a published object,
    such as a paper, dataset or code deposit, written like
    `10.5281/zenodo.1234567`. Adding `https://doi.org/` in front gives a link
    that keeps working even if the object's web address changes. Repositories
    such as Zenodo and Figshare assign one when you deposit. See
    [Available](#available).

[Documented]{#gloss-documented}
:   The third TADA principle: a README and a licence describe the code, its
    software environment, where the data are and how to run it. See
    [Documented](#documented).

[Double-blind review]{#gloss-double-blind data-match="double-blind"}
:   Peer review in which neither the authors nor the reviewers know who the
    others are. Code and READMEs have to be anonymised for it. See
    [Anonymising for double-blind review](#available-anonymous).

[Embargo]{#gloss-embargo data-match="embargo"}
:   A period during which an archived deposit exists but is not yet public.
    Many repositories offer one for sensitive data.

[Environment manager]{#gloss-environment-manager data-match="environment manager|dependency manager|renv|conda|poetry|pipenv|groundhog"}
:   A tool that records and restores the exact package versions a project uses,
    usually in a *lockfile*. `renv` (R) and `conda`, `poetry` and `pipenv`
    (Python) are examples. Beyond the scope of TADA.

[FAIR principles]{#gloss-fair data-match="FAIR"} [SORTEE]{.tada-gloss-tag}
:   Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable: principles for sharing
    data and code ([Wilkinson et al. 2016]{.tada-cite data-key="wilkinson-2016"}).
    See [How TADA maps onto FAIR](#tada-fair).

[FAIR4RS]{#gloss-fair4rs data-match="FAIR4RS"}
:   The FAIR principles adapted for research software
    ([Chue Hong et al. 2022]{.tada-cite data-key="chue-hong-2022"}).

[File extension]{#gloss-extension data-match="file extension|extension"}
:   The ending of a file name, such as `.R`, `.py` or `.csv`, which tells
    software what kind of file it is. See
    [Transferable](#transferable-filetype).

[GitHub]{#gloss-github data-match="GitHub"}
:   A website for developing code with version control and collaborating on it.
    It is not an archive, because files can be changed or deleted and it does
    not give a persistent identifier. See
    [Why GitHub is not an archive](#available-github).

[IDE]{#gloss-ide data-match="IDE"}
:   Integrated development environment: an application for writing and running
    code, such as RStudio, Positron, VS Code, PyCharm or Spyder.

[Immutable]{#gloss-immutable data-match="immutable|immutability"}
:   Cannot be changed or deleted once published. In an immutable repository,
    such as Zenodo, an update creates a new version instead of overwriting the
    old one, so the exact files behind a paper stay available. GitHub and OSF
    are not immutable.

[Interoperable]{#gloss-interoperable data-match="interoperable|interoperability"}
:   Able to be opened and used across different software and operating systems.
    Plain-text formats such as `.csv` for data and `.R` or `.py` for code are
    interoperable; `.xls`, `.docx` and `.pdf` are not. The "I" in FAIR.

[Licence]{#gloss-licence data-match="licence|license|licensing|licensed"}
:   A statement of what others may legally do with your code or data. Without
    one, others cannot lawfully reuse it, even if they can see it. See
    [The licence](#documented-licence).

[Lockfile]{#gloss-lockfile data-match="lockfile|lock file|renv.lock"}
:   A file written by an environment manager (for example `renv.lock`) that
    records the exact version of every package a project uses.

[MCMC]{#gloss-mcmc data-match="MCMC"}
:   Markov chain Monte Carlo, a family of stochastic sampling methods, common in
    Bayesian models. Results differ slightly between runs unless a *seed* is
    set.

[MeRIT]{#gloss-merit data-match="MeRIT"}
:   Method Reporting with Initials for Transparency: adding the initials of the
    person who did each step to the methods section, for example "Code was
    checked by E.I.C."
    ([Nakagawa et al. 2023]{.tada-cite data-key="nakagawa-2023"}).

[Metadata]{#gloss-metadata data-match="metadata"} [SORTEE]{.tada-gloss-tag}
:   A description of, and information about, the data and code. Usually a text
    file called a README, sometimes with a data dictionary.

[Namespace]{#gloss-namespace data-match="namespace"}
:   The package a function belongs to. Calling a function with its namespace,
    as in `dplyr::filter()`, shows the reader which package it comes from.

[PEP 8]{#gloss-pep8 data-match="PEP 8|PEP8"}
:   The standard style guide for Python code.

[Permissive licence]{#gloss-permissive data-match="permissive"}
:   A licence with few conditions, usually just that the licence and copyright
    notice are kept. MIT, BSD and Apache 2.0 are examples. Compare *copyleft
    licence*.

[Persistent identifier (PID)]{#gloss-pid data-match="persistent identifier|PID"}
:   A globally unique, long-lasting reference to a digital object that keeps
    pointing to it even if it moves. DOIs are the most common kind; others
    include SWHIDs, ARKs, Handles, RRIDs and accession numbers such as those
    from GenBank. A GitHub URL is not one.

[Processed data]{#gloss-processed-data}
:   Data that have been through *data processing*.

[Project]{#gloss-project} [SORTEE]{.tada-gloss-tag}
:   The collection of files archived for one manuscript. GitHub calls this a
    *repository*, which causes some confusion; see *repository*.

[Proprietary format]{#gloss-proprietary data-match="proprietary"}
:   A file format controlled by one company and needing its software to open,
    such as `.xls` or SPSS `.sav`. The opposite of an interoperable format.

[Pull request]{#gloss-pull-request data-match="pull request"}
:   On GitHub, a proposed change to a repository that others can review and
    comment on before it is merged.

[Raw data]{#gloss-raw-data data-match="raw data"} [SORTEE]{.tada-gloss-tag}
:   Unprocessed and unfiltered data, including raw files such as photos, audio
    recordings, videos and data sheets.

[README]{#gloss-readme data-match="README"}
:   A plain-text file (`README.md` or `README.txt`) at the top of a project
    that says what the project is, what each file does and how to run it. See
    [The README](#documented-readme).

[Relative path]{#gloss-relative-path data-match="relative path|relative file path"}
:   A file path written from the top of the project folder, such as
    `data/raw/counts.csv`. It works on any computer, wherever the folder sits.
    Compare *absolute path*.

[Release]{#gloss-release data-match="release"}
:   On GitHub, a named, fixed snapshot of a repository. Zenodo can archive each
    release and give it a DOI.

[Repository]{#gloss-repository data-match="repository|repositories"} [SORTEE]{.tada-gloss-tag}
:   A service that stores many projects for the long term, such as Zenodo,
    Dryad or Figshare. On GitHub the word means a single project instead.

[Seed]{#gloss-seed data-match="seed"}
:   A number that fixes the starting point of a random number generator, so
    stochastic code generates the same pseudorandom numbers, and gives the
    same result, each run. Set with `set.seed()` in R
    or `random.seed()` in Python.

[Session info]{#gloss-session-info data-match="sessionInfo|session_info|session info"}
:   A printout of the software environment: language version, operating system
    and every loaded package with its version. Produced by `sessionInfo()` in R
    or `session_info` in Python.

[Software]{#gloss-software}
:   Code written to be general, modular and tested, so it works across systems
    and on many datasets. Compare *analytical code*.

[Stochastic]{#gloss-stochastic data-match="stochastic"}
:   Involving randomness, so the output can differ between runs. Simulations,
    bootstrapping and MCMC are stochastic.

[Supplementary material]{#gloss-supplementary data-match="supplementary material"}
:   Files attached to a journal article. Not an archive: it has no persistent
    identifier of its own and may not stay open and accessible.

[SWHID]{#gloss-swhid data-match="SWHID|Software Heritage"}
:   SoftWare Hash IDentifier, the persistent identifier used by Software
    Heritage to reference archived source code.

[Transferable]{#gloss-transferable}
:   The first TADA principle: anyone can open and run your code on their own
    computer without converting or editing it. See
    [Transferable](#transferable).

[Unit test]{#gloss-unit-test data-match="unit test|unit testing"}
:   A small automated check that a function gives the expected output for a
    known input, written with `testthat` (R) or `pytest` (Python).

[Virtual environment]{#gloss-virtual-environment data-match="virtual environment"}
:   In Python, a self-contained setup for one project with its own packages,
    kept separate from the rest of the computer.

[Working directory]{#gloss-working-directory data-match="working directory|setwd"}
:   The folder R or Python treats as its starting point when reading and saving
    files. Opening an RStudio project sets it to the project folder.

[Workflow manager]{#gloss-workflow-manager data-match="workflow manager|Snakemake|Nextflow"}
:   A tool that runs the steps of an analysis in a defined order and tracks
    which steps depend on which, such as Snakemake or Nextflow. Beyond the
    scope of TADA.

:::

Missing a term? See [Contribute](#contribute).
